common_name: Autauga Crimson Clover (Early-Maturing Reseeding Southern Cover Crop Clover)

planting.note: Broadcast onto a firm, weed-free seedbed in early fall; Autauga is grouped among the earlier-maturing reseeding crimson clovers alongside Dixie and Auburn, flowering and setting seed before later-maturing types such as Talladega.

directions: Autauga is one of the early-maturing reseeding crimson clover cultivars grown in the Southeast alongside Dixie and Auburn, flowering and setting hard seed before later-maturing types such as Talladega extend the bloom window into late spring. Broadcast or drill seed onto a firm, weed-free seedbed in early fall so plants build a strong root system ahead of winter. Like other reseeding crimson clovers, it fixes nitrogen through fall and winter growth and can be terminated at early bloom for maximum nitrogen release, or allowed to mature and shatter seed to sustain a self-reseeding stand in following years.

common_name: Ananas Yokneam Melon (White-Fleshed Smooth-Skinned Israeli Ananas Melon)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost in warm, deeply enriched soil; Ananas Yokneam is the traditional Israeli strain of Ananas melon, distinguished by its smooth white skin and white flesh rather than the netted, orange-fleshed French type.

directions: Ananas Yokneam is the traditional Israeli regional strain of Ananas ('pineapple') melon, distinguished from the netted, orange-fleshed French Ananas type by its smooth white skin and white flesh. Like other Ananas melons it is prized for an intensely aromatic, spicy-sweet fragrance that has been compared to pineapple, vanilla, and spiced honey, perfuming a room when a ripe fruit is present. Sow in hills or rows after last frost in deeply enriched, well-drained soil and provide 6-8 feet of row space or a strong trellis with hammock-style fruit support. Favor dry growing conditions where possible, since wet weather can dilute the fragrance and flavor that distinguish this strain.

common_name: Goldberg Golden Purslane (Large Golden-Yellow-Leaved Culinary Purslane)

planting.note: Direct sow thickly in warm soil (70F+) in well-drained soil in full sun; Goldberg is a named golden purslane cultivar distinguished by unusually large, golden-yellow leaves.

directions: Goldberg is a named cultivar of golden purslane distinguished by unusually large, golden-yellow leaves, grown alongside the more upright, green-leaved 'Gruner' as one of the two most commonly named selections of culinary purslane. Scatter seed on warm, bare soil and press in lightly, since seed needs some light to germinate; thin to 4-6 inches or harvest as a cut-and-come-again crop. Like other golden purslane selections it thrives in the summer heat and drought that cause most other salad greens to bolt, and its succulent, mildly tart leaves are notably rich in omega-3 fatty acids, vitamin C, and beta-carotene.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Summer Vegetables

common_name: Gruner Golden Purslane (Upright Green-Leaved Culinary Purslane)

planting.note: Direct sow thickly in warm soil (70F+) in well-drained soil in full sun; Gruner is a named golden purslane cultivar with green leaves and a more upright habit than other golden purslane selections.

directions: Gruner is a named cultivar of golden purslane with green rather than golden-yellow leaves and a more upright habit than other golden purslane selections, grown alongside the large, golden-leaved 'Goldberg' as one of the two most commonly named culinary purslane cultivars. Scatter seed on warm, bare soil and press in lightly, since seed needs some light to germinate; thin to 4-6 inches or harvest as a cut-and-come-again crop. Its more upright growth habit makes it easier to harvest by hand than sprawling purslane types, while it retains the same heat tolerance, drought tolerance, and high omega-3 content that make golden purslane an outstanding summer salad green.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Summer Vegetables

common_name: Ohno Scarlet Turnip (Rare Older Japanese Red Turnip, Parent of Scarlet Ohno Revival)

planting.note: Direct sow in late summer or fall for fall harvest; Ohno Scarlet is the older, once-rare Japanese turnip variety from which seed savers selected the modern Scarlet Ohno Revival.

directions: Ohno Scarlet is the older, once-rare Japanese heirloom turnip that seed savers selected from to create the modern Scarlet Ohno Revival, which takes its name directly from this parent variety and was bred to bring back a type that had become scarce in seed collections. Sow directly 1/4 inch deep in late summer or fall and thin seedlings to 4-6 inches apart for best root development. As with its better-known descendant, both the root and leaves are traditionally used in the kitchen rather than the root alone.
